note: In Canto 15 Dante learned that his ancestor was knighted by an emperor and died on crusade. He admits that the news made him proud of his family, even in Heaven.
Nobility wears out unless each generation adds worth of its own. In his earlier book, the Convivio, Dante had argued that true nobility comes from a person's virtue, not from birth.

The Italian voi, the plural used as a mark of respect to one person. Until now Dante has addressed his ancestor with the familiar tu. Medieval tradition held that the plural was first used in Rome, to honor Julius Caesar. By Dante's time the Romans themselves were known for saying tu to everyone.

The Lady of Malehaut, in the Old French romance of Lancelot. She coughed to let the lovers know she had seen their first secret meeting. Beatrice's smile tells Dante, just as gently, that she has caught his little vanity.
King Arthur's queen, who loved the knight Lancelot. Her "first sin" is their first kiss, the same scene Francesca and Paolo were reading in Inferno 5.

context: In the Italian, this line and the next two each begin with the respectful voi.
John the Baptist is the city's patron saint, so Florence is his sheepfold. Dante asks about the city of his ancestor's youth, about two hundred years before.

note: Usually read as the older Florentine of his own day, two centuries before Dante. Dante held that a living language keeps changing. Some take it to mean Latin, which the spirit spoke at first in Canto 15.
The angel Gabriel's greeting to Mary at the Annunciation, when Christ was conceived. Florence began its year on that feast, 25 March, and counted its years from it.
The planet Mars, where they are standing. It comes back to the constellation Leo, the Lion, once in each trip around the sky, which the astronomy books Dante used put at about 687 days.

The text of the poem most editors accept gives the number as 580. That many returns of Mars, at 687 days each, puts the birth in about 1091. An old variant reading has 553, which was once paired with a rough two-year orbit to give 1106.

quote: the runner in your annual race
note: The palio, a horse race run across Florence each year on the feast of John the Baptist, 24 June. The last district the riders entered was Porta San Piero, in the oldest part of the city. Dante's family still had its houses there.

quote: silence is more gracious than speech
note: Either modesty, after the opening rebuke of family pride, or a sign that nothing more was known. Nothing certain is recorded of Dante's family before this ancestor.
The two ends of the old city. An ancient statue said to be of Mars stood by the Ponte Vecchio on the river, to the south. The Baptistery of Saint John stood near the northern wall.
Small towns in the countryside around Florence. Figghine is now called Figline. Their people had moved into the city as it grew, and the old families looked down on them.
Two villages a few miles from the center, one to the south and one to the north. The speaker wishes Florence had never spread its rule beyond them.

Baldo d'Aguglione, a lawyer from a village near Florence who rose high in the city. He was caught up in a scandal over tampering with public records in 1299. In 1311 he drew up an amnesty for exiles that left Dante out by name.
Usually identified as Fazio dei Morubaldini of Signa, a lawyer and politician accused of selling favors. He went over from the White Guelphs to the Blacks, Dante's enemies.
The clergy, and above all the papal court. Dante held that the Church, by fighting the emperors, had left Italy without a ruler and thrown its towns and countryside into disorder.
The emperor. In Dante's time this was the Holy Roman Emperor, whom he saw as the rightful heir of the Caesars.
A fortified hill town southwest of Florence. The Florentines captured and destroyed it in 1202, and its people came to the city. Which newcomer the speaker has in mind is not known.
A castle in the hills between Prato and Pistoia. Its owners, the Counts Guidi, could not hold it against Pistoia and sold it to Florence in 1254.
A family of country origin, from Acone in the valley of the Sieve, who grew very rich as merchants and bankers in Florence. By 1300 they led the White Guelphs, the party Dante was exiled with.
Lords of a castle in the valley of the Greve, south of Florence. The city destroyed it in 1135 and made the family live in town. The harm that followed is told at the end of the canto.
A large city that loses its way falls harder than a small one. The single sword that cuts better than five answers the boast of size: Florence in 1300 had five times the men, and was weaker for it.
Two Roman cities that lay in ruins by Dante's time. Luni stood on the coast where Tuscany meets Liguria. Urbisaglia was in the Marche, in central Italy.

Once one of the great Etruscan cities, in the south of Tuscany. In Dante's time it was sunk in malarial marsh. Sinigaglia, on the Adriatic coast, had been emptied by war and fever. Both survive today.

quote: the turning of the moon's sphere
note: The tides. Medieval science knew that they follow the moon, which was thought to be carried around the earth by a turning sphere of its own.

The first of some forty old Florentine families named in the rest of the canto. Most had died out or sunk low by 1300, which is the point of the list. The Ughi left their name on a church in the city and on the hill of Montughi outside it.
A very old house that was barely remembered in Dante's time.
The chronicler Giovanni Villani, who was Dante's younger contemporary, says they had been great and powerful and had come to nothing.
The street called Borgo dei Greci in Florence still carries their name. The family had gone from the city by Dante's time.
They lived where the city's great public palace, now the Palazzo Vecchio, was later built. Villani says that in his day they were called the Foraboschi.
They had their own church, Santa Maria degli Alberighi, near Dante's home. By his time the family was extinct.
An old house that still existed in 1300 but had lost its standing.
The dell'Arca, an old house that had died out by Dante's time.
The Soldanieri, a Ghibelline house. One of them, Gianni, is among the traitors frozen in the ice in Inferno 32. He turned on his own party in 1266.
Two more old houses of the city center, both much reduced by 1300.

Porta San Piero, the eastern gate of the old city. By 1300 the houses there belonged to the Cerchi, leaders of the White Guelphs. Their "treachery" is the party strife they brought on Florence. The ship is the city, and the throwing overboard is the exile of the Whites in 1302.
The family of Bellincione Berti. It died out in the male line, and its houses by the gate passed to the Counts Guidi and then, by sale, to the Cerchi.

context: Bellincione's daughter Gualdrada married Count Guido the Elder. Their grandson Guido Guerra is among the Florentines Dante honors in Inferno 16.
His other daughters married into Florentine houses, and their descendants took up his name with pride.

note: The della Pressa, a family that already held public office in the city.
The Galigai, a Ghibelline house. A gilded sword hilt and pommel were the marks of a knight, so the family already had knights in it.
The coat of arms of the Pigli family: a vertical stripe of vair on a red field. Vair is the heraldic pattern that stands for squirrel fur.

A Guelph house. Early commentators say it had a blood feud with Dante's family: a Sacchetti killed Dante's cousin Geri del Bello, whom Dante meets in Inferno 29. The storyteller Franco Sacchetti was born into it a generation after Dante.
A Ghibelline house, fallen from the nobility by Dante's time.
A Ghibelline house. One of them was among the men who killed Buondelmonte in the murder told at the end of this canto.
An old house that had died out by Dante's time.
An old house of the city center, fallen low by 1300.

quote: those who blush for the false bushel
note: The Chiaramontesi. One of them, in charge of the city's salt, gave it out in a bushel measure made smaller by removing a stave, and kept the difference. The same fraud is recalled in Purgatorio 12.

quote: The stock that bore the Calfucci
context: The Calfucci were a branch of the Donati and had died out by Dante's time.

note: The Sizii and the Arrigucci were old houses whose men held the highest offices in the city. The curule chair was the seat of the chief magistrates in ancient Rome.
The Uberti, the leading Ghibelline house of Florence. After the Guelphs won, the family was banished for good and its houses were torn down. Its great man, Farinata, speaks with Dante in Inferno 10.
The coat of arms of the Lamberti: gold balls on a blue field. Mosca de' Lamberti, who urged the murder that split the city, is in Inferno 28.

The Visdomini and the Tosinghi, hereditary guardians of the bishopric of Florence. Whenever a bishop died, they ran its property until a new one was named, and were said to live well off it meanwhile.
The Adimari. Filippo Argenti, the furious soul of Inferno 8, belonged to them. Early commentators say that one of the family took over Dante's property after his exile and worked against his return.
A Donati who married a daughter of Bellincione Berti. He was annoyed when Bellincione gave another daughter to one of the Adimari, which made that upstart house his relations.
The Caponsacchi, a Ghibelline house from the hill town of Fiesole, who settled by the Old Market in the center of Florence. The mother of Dante's Beatrice came from this family.
Heads of the Giudi and the Infangati, two Ghibelline houses.

The first ring of city walls. One of its gates, the Porta Peruzza, was named for the della Pera. Incredible, either because so great a family was by 1300 forgotten, or because the old city was so free of envy that it let a gate carry a private family's name.

Hugh, margrave of Tuscany, who died on the feast of Saint Thomas, 21 December 1001. He was buried in the Badia, the abbey of Florence, where the monks honored his memory each year on that day. Several families he had knighted carried versions of his red and white striped arms.

quote: he who borders it with a band
note: Giano della Bella, whose family bore Hugh's arms with a gold border. Though a noble, he led the popular government and in 1293 brought in the Ordinances of Justice, which shut the great families out of office. He was driven into exile in 1295.
Two families of the Borgo Santi Apostoli, a street near the river.
Borgo Santi Apostoli. The new neighbors are the Buondelmonti, who settled there when they were made to move into the city.

quote: The house from which your weeping springs
note: The Amidei. Buondelmonte was pledged to marry a girl of their house and jilted her. The Amidei and their allies killed him for it, and Florence split into two armed camps.

context: The "other" who urged him was a lady of the Donati, who offered him her own daughter in place of the Amidei bride.

note: A small river on the road from the family's old castle to Florence. Better for the city if the first Buondelmonte to come had drowned in it on the way.

The broken statue said to be of Mars, at the foot of the Ponte Vecchio. Buondelmonte was killed beside it on Easter morning. Mars was held to be the city's first patron, before John the Baptist, so the murder looks like a sacrifice to the god of war. Inferno 13 tells of the statue's grudge against Florence.
The old flag of Florence was a white lily on a red field. It was never "reversed": no enemy had ever captured it and dragged it upside down in triumph.

context: In 1251 the Guelphs, having driven out the Ghibellines, changed the city's flag to a red lily on white. The Ghibellines kept the old white lily on red.
